title: Vision of the New Temple
overview: Ezekiel 40 presents a detailed visionary tour of a future temple complex in Jerusalem, given to the prophet during the Babylonian exile. The chapter marks the beginning of a series of visions describing the restoration of Israel’s worship and the presence of God among His people. The vision includes precise measurements of gates, courts, chambers, and architectural features, emphasizing order, holiness, and divine design. This chapter is foundational for understanding the eschatological hope of Israel’s restoration and the renewed relationship between God and His people. It sets the stage for the temple’s significance as a symbol of God's dwelling and the center of worship in the coming kingdom.
structure:
**Verses 1-2: The Vision's Setting.** Ezekiel is transported in a divine vision to the land of Israel, placed on a high mountain overlooking a city, symbolizing a vantage point for the revelation of the temple’s design.

**Verses 3-16: Introduction to the Measuring Man and Eastern Gate.** A man with the appearance of brass appears with measuring tools, signifying divine authority and precision. He begins by measuring the outer wall and the eastern gate, detailing the dimensions and architectural features.

**Verses 17-27: Measurements of the Outer Courts and Gates.** The vision continues with measurements of the outward courts and gates facing north and south, including chambers, windows, arches, and decorative palm trees, highlighting the temple’s grandeur and sacred order.

**Verses 28-37: Inner Court Gates and Their Features.** The inner court gates are measured with similar detail, emphasizing symmetry and the sacred function of these entrances, including steps and palm tree decorations.

**Verses 38-43: Chambers for Sacrificial Preparation.** The chapter describes chambers near the gates for washing burnt offerings and tables for sacrifices, underscoring the temple’s role in worship and atonement.

**Verses 44-46: Chambers for Priests and Singers.** Specific chambers are designated for the priests and singers, particularly the sons of Zadok, highlighting the priestly service and worship leadership.

**Verses 47-49: Measurements of the Inner Court and Porch.** The chapter concludes with measurements of the inner court and the porch of the temple, reinforcing the temple’s sacred architecture and the orderly approach to God’s presence.

keyVerses.text: And he brought me thither, and, behold, there was a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass, with a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate.
keyVerses.significance: This verse introduces the measuring man, a divine messenger symbolizing God’s authority and the precision required in the temple’s design. It underscores the holiness and orderliness of God’s dwelling place.

keyVerses.text: And the man said unto me, Son of man, behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears, and set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee; for to the intent that I might shew them unto thee art thou brought hither: declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the prophetic commission given to Ezekiel to observe carefully and report the vision to Israel, emphasizing the importance of the temple vision for Israel’s restoration and hope.

keyVerses.text: And behold a wall on the outside of the house round about, and in the man's hand a measuring reed of six cubits long by the cubit and an hand breadth: so he measured the breadth of the building, one reed; and the height, one reed.
keyVerses.significance: The precise measurements signify God’s detailed plan for the temple, symbolizing divine order and the perfection required in approaching God’s holy presence.

keyVerses.text: So he measured the court, an hundred cubits long, and an hundred cubits broad, foursquare; and the altar that was before the house.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the temple court’s perfect symmetry and the centrality of the altar, underscoring the importance of worship and sacrifice in the restored relationship between God and His people.

characters.name: Ezekiel
characters.description: The prophet receiving the vision, tasked with observing and reporting the detailed measurements and features of the new temple to the exiled Israelites, symbolizing hope and restoration.

characters.name: The Man with the Measuring Reed
characters.description: A divine messenger with the appearance of brass who guides Ezekiel through the temple, measuring its gates and courts with precision, representing God’s authority and the holiness of the temple.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes God’s holiness through precise measurements and orderly design of the temple, reflecting the sacred nature of God’s dwelling and the need for reverence in worship.
Ezekiel’s vision points to the future restoration of Israel’s temple and worship after exile, symbolizing God’s promise to dwell again with His people and renew their covenant relationship.
The detailed temple vision underscores the central biblical theme of God’s presence dwelling among His people, a key hope for Israel’s spiritual renewal and ultimate redemption.

historicalContext: Ezekiel 40 is set during the Babylonian exile, approximately 25 years after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. The Jewish people were living in captivity, mourning the loss of their temple and city. The vision reflects a future hope for restoration and rebuilding of the temple, which was the center of Jewish worship and national identity. The geographical setting is the land of Israel, with the prophet placed on a high mountain overlooking a city, symbolizing a vantage point for divine revelation. The detailed architectural descriptions reflect ancient Near Eastern temple design customs and the importance of sacred space in Israelite religion. Politically, Israel was under Babylonian control, and this vision offered hope for divine intervention and renewal.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theologians often see Ezekiel 40 as a prophetic vision pointing to the ultimate fulfillment in the New Testament church, where God’s presence dwells spiritually among His people rather than in a physical temple.

Dispensationalists interpret this chapter literally, expecting a future millennial temple to be built in Jerusalem as part of God’s covenantal promises to Israel, emphasizing the physical restoration of the nation.

Early church interpreters often viewed the temple vision allegorically, seeing the temple as a symbol of Christ’s body or the heavenly sanctuary, focusing on spiritual worship and the presence of God in the believer.

crossReferences.connection: Describes Solomon’s temple dimensions, providing a historical precedent for temple measurements and design, which Ezekiel’s vision expands upon.
Mentions the New Jerusalem having no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, connecting to Ezekiel’s theme of God’s presence among His people.
God commands Moses to build the tabernacle according to divine pattern, paralleling the detailed measurements and divine instructions in Ezekiel’s vision.
Expresses the longing for God’s house, reflecting the spiritual significance of the temple as a place of God’s presence, echoed in Ezekiel’s vision.
Speaks of Christ as the high priest entering the heavenly sanctuary, connecting the earthly temple’s symbolism to Christ’s ultimate priestly work.

application: Trust in God’s sovereign plan for restoration even in times of loss and exile, knowing He will fulfill His promises.
Approach God with reverence and holiness, recognizing the sacredness of His presence in our lives.
Value order and obedience in worship, following God’s instructions carefully as a sign of respect and devotion.
Encourage the church community to anticipate the fulfillment of God’s kingdom and the ultimate dwelling of God with His people.
Commit to spiritual preparation and cleansing, as the temple’s chambers for offerings remind believers of the need for holiness.
Use detailed study of Scripture to deepen understanding of God’s plans and purposes, as Ezekiel carefully observed and reported the vision.
conclusion: Ezekiel 40 offers a profound vision of hope and restoration for God’s people through the detailed revelation of a new temple. It highlights God’s holiness, the importance of worship, and the promise of His abiding presence among His people. For believers today, this chapter calls for reverence, faithfulness, and anticipation of God’s ultimate fulfillment of His covenant promises. The temple’s precise measurements remind us that God’s plans are perfect and that our worship must be orderly and sincere. This vision encourages Christians to live in hopeful expectation of God’s kingdom, where He will dwell fully with His people forever.
timeline: c. 573 BC - Vision during Babylonian exile, 25 years after Jerusalem’s destruction (586 BC)

A measuring rod used in ancient times, often about six cubits long, used here to describe temple dimensions.
An entrance area or vestibule leading into a building, here referring to the temple’s gate entrances.
Decorative carvings or motifs symbolizing victory, peace, and eternal life, used here as ornamentation on temple posts.
A type of sacrifice completely consumed by fire, symbolizing atonement and dedication to God.

outline.heading: The Vision’s Setting and Introduction of the Measuring Man
outline.description: Ezekiel is brought in a vision to a high mountain overlooking a city and meets a man with a measuring reed who begins to measure the temple’s outer wall and gate, symbolizing divine authority and precision.

outline.heading: Measurements of the Eastern Gate and Outer Chambers
outline.description: Detailed measurements of the eastern gate’s thresholds, chambers, porches, and decorative features are given, emphasizing the temple’s grandeur and sacred order.

outline.heading: Outer Courts and Gates Facing North and South
outline.description: The vision continues with measurements of the outer courts and gates toward the north and south, including chambers, windows, arches, and palm tree decorations, highlighting symmetry and holiness.

outline.heading: Inner Court Gates and Their Features
outline.description: The inner court gates are measured with similar detail, including steps and palm tree decorations, underscoring the sacredness of these entrances.

outline.heading: Sacrificial Chambers and Tables
outline.description: Chambers near the gates for washing burnt offerings and tables for sacrifices are described, illustrating the temple’s role in worship and atonement.

outline.heading: Priestly Chambers and Final Measurements of the Inner Court
outline.description: Chambers for priests and singers are designated, and the inner court and porch are measured, reinforcing the temple’s sacred architecture and orderly approach to God’s presence.
